newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU seek to resolve split on technology pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU seek to resolve split on technology pact.

text.p: U.S. and European Union trade chiefs said on Thursday they hoped to settle differences over an information technology deal both sides want approved at the World Trade Organisation ministers' meeting in December.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who last week accused Europe of backing away from an agreement to eliminate tariffs on a wide range of electronic products, and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said they made some progress at a meeting late on Thursday.

"We haven't resolved it yet," Brittan told reporters following the one-on-one session with Barshefsky. "We're quite happy to negotiate to drop tariffs, but there have to be other things in the agreement as well."

Barshefsky and Brittan were in Seattle to attend a meeting of Quadrilateral trade ministers which also includes Canada's Arthur Eggleton and Japan's Shunpei Tsukahara. Barshefsky said Quad leadership on a technology deal was needed to win a global agreement at the first meeting of World Trade Organisation ministers to be held in Singapore in December.
She said "good progress" was made at Thursday's meeting with Brittan and she hoped their differences could be resolved by the time the four trade chiefs leave Seattle on Saturday.
Barshefsky said early on Thursday the main stumbling block was a lack of agreement among the members of the EU.

"Clearly Europe has to come to a rapid decision on this issue. We will not be able to move forward on this initiative ... without Europe because we will not let Europe free ride on our tariff reductions," she said.
The Information Technology Agreement (ITA) would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of information products including computer chips, software and telecommunications equipment.
"We want the ITA to be agreed to in Singapore," said a European Union spokesman.
Brittan said the main obstacle to reaching accord on the global technology agreement was the U.S.-Japan semiconductor arrangement, which excludes Europe.
"We are not prepared to see the U.S., Japan discriminating agreement go ahead unconditionally," Brittan said.

Earlier this week, the EU wrote a letter to Barshefsky suggesting that work on the ITA could begin if the "discriminatory aspects" of the U.S.-Japan chip alliance, which was renewed this summer, were not applied until after the ITA was finalised, according to officials in Brussels.

But Barshefsky has said the semiconductor issue can be easily resolved and that Europe appears to be backing away from the ITA because it does not have full agreement among its members. Brittan has denied that Europe is backing away from the ITA.

U.S. government and industry officials have said that some EU member states are seeking other trade concessions as a price for ending duties on information technology even though European electronic companies are willing to see tariffs dropped.
